grammar.title: Frase
grammar.rule: Eu trabalho; nós trabalhamos. Ana e Bia trabalham juntas.
grammar.note_en:
Nós means “we”: it includes the speaker and one or more other people. Ana says Nós trabalhamos juntas, Bia (“We work together, Bia”), including herself and Bia. Eu trabalho com você means “I work with you”; nós trabalhamos means “we work.” Vocês means “you” addressed to more than one listener. Rosa says Vocês colocam as três cadeiras perto da mesa (“You put the three chairs near the table”), addressing Paulo and the neighbor; then Ana e Bia, vocês ajudam também? means “Ana and Bia, do you help too?” The audience can change. The named people and speech context establish who belongs to each group.

Eles means “they” for a masculine or mixed group, elas for a feminine group. In the first section, Ana e Bia pegam o papel means “Ana and Bia take the paper”; Elas colocam a cadeira means “They put the chair,” with elas referring to those two women. O vizinho e Paulo pegam uma cadeira juntos means “The neighbor and Paulo take a chair together”; Eles têm três cadeiras means “They have three chairs.” Juntas/juntos agrees with the people acting together: juntas for Ana and Bia, juntos for Paulo and the neighbor. It does not describe whether a feminine or masculine chair is carried.

Plural subjects now take plural verbs. The verb agrees with who performs the action, not with the objects: Rosa coloca cinco cadeiras means “Rosa puts five chairs [in position]”; Ana e Bia colocam uma cadeira means “Ana and Bia put one chair [in position].” The number of chairs does not decide coloca/colocam. Regular -ar verbs replace the dictionary ending -ar with -amos for nós and -am for eles/elas/vocês: colocar → colocamos/colocam (“put → we put/they or you put”), trabalhar → trabalhamos/trabalham (“work → we work/they or you work”). A dictionary form labels the action; it is not an extra sentence tense. Use only the encountered cells, rather than guessing all persons from these examples.

The other regular patterns met here are -er and -ir. Comer becomes comemos for nós (“we eat”); beber becomes bebemos (“we drink”); dividir becomes dividimos (“we divide/share”). With a singular named person, Ana come means “Ana eats” and Bia bebe means “Bia drinks.” Eating is shown without an object here; café is what they drink. Do not read Nós comemos aqui e bebemos café (“We eat here and drink coffee”) as eating coffee. Dividir a mesa means sharing/dividing the available table space, not cutting the furniture: Nós dividimos a mesa means “We share the table.” Elas dividem a mesa means “They share the table.” Escreve/escrevem means “writes/write”; Bia escreve no papel means “Bia writes on the paper.” These regular endings name particular demonstrated forms, not permission to invent other verbs.

Several frequent verbs require their actual forms. Nós temos means “we have,” eles têm “they have”; the plural têm has a circumflex, unlike singular tem. Nós estamos means “we are,” as cadeiras estão means “the chairs are”; vocês veem means “you see.” Ler is not a model for all regular -er endings: eu leio means “I read,” Bia lê “Bia reads,” nós lemos “we read,” Bia e Rosa leem “Bia and Rosa read.” Leem and veem have two e letters and no circumflex in this Brazilian spelling. Nós precisamos de espaço means “we need space,” preserving the de already taught with precisar. Plural subjects do not remove the preposition.

Caber means fitting within available capacity. The chapter uses only cabe with one thing and cabem with more than one: O caderno cabe means “The notebook fits”; Os três livros cabem na mesa means “The three books fit on the table”; As cadeiras não cabem aqui means “The chairs do not fit here.” Capacity includes usable access: filling the doorway with a chair does not make a workable reading room. Tirar removes something from its current place, while colocar puts it into a place: Ana tira a cadeira da porta means “Ana removes the chair from the doorway”; Elas colocam a cadeira perto da mesa means “They put the chair near the table.” Do not treat the two verbs as interchangeable.

A vizinho is a male neighbor; living near the café and Rosa establishes that relation here, rather than friendship alone. Pátio means “courtyard,” an outdoor space, shown in the neighbor’s phone photograph. The conversation proposes sharing it. The story does not yet visit it, hold the reading evening, buy chairs or remove a participant’s name. Five café chairs plus one borrowed chair remain; two borrowed chairs are returned. Putting books on the table and moving chairs are distinct tests of available space.

In the table, trabalha means “works” with one named person, while trabalhamos means “we work” and trabalham “they/you work.” Tem means “has” with one named person, versus temos “we have” and têm “they/you have.” Escrevem/dividem use the encountered group ending -em, giving “they/you write” and “they/you share”; abrem means “they open,” compared with singular abre (“opens”). The table’s Ana/Rosa column contains singular named-person forms, not eu forms.
